# 8Q

[](https://github.com/Spooky-Manufacturing/8Q#contributors-)

[](https://zenodo.org/badge/latestdoi/275711975)

Computer with built-in General Purpose 8 Qubit Optical Quantum Processor

# Contributors

Thank you to all the contributors who make this possible

# Status: Moving Towards PCB!

We're beginning to layout the components and finalize the design of our quantum computer! As we continue to design the PCB, we are also working with optical engineers to make our logic gates more compact which will enable us to shrink the design even further than we already have!

### Development Board

To speed up R&D, we've decided to replace the ARM CPU with a QSeven2.0 spec'd "computer on module". There are a variety of benefits to doing this, one major benefit being that we can switch between a variety of x86 and ARM processors.

The current design effort utilizes the Congatech A50 CoM.

[](https://github.com/Spooky-Manufacturing/8Q/blob/master/docs/source/imgs/cpu.png)

### Quantum Processing Unit

[](https://github.com/Spooky-Manufacturing/8Q/blob/master/docs/source/imgs/qpu.png)

### QController

The QController acts as a bridge between the main (digital) computer and the quantum processor. It is responsible for storing/executing instructions, and for transferring data to/from the host and QPU.

## Features

[](https://github.com/Spooky-Manufacturing/8Q/blob/master/docs/source/imgs/8q.png)

* Quad-Core Cortex-A53

# Python Packaging Authority¶

The Python Packaging Authority (PyPA) is a working group that maintains a core
set of software projects used in Python packaging.

The software developed through the PyPA is used to package, share, and install
Python software and to interact with indexes of downloadable Python software
such as PyPI, the Python Package Index. Click the logo below to download pip, the most prominent software used to interact with PyPI.

[](https://pypi.org/project/pip/#files)

on how to package, publish, and install Python projects using current
tools**. The User Guide provides a user introduction to packaging, and
explains how to use these tools. In case you need to package Python
with other languages (for example, in a scientific Python package),
the user guide also offers basic information about and links to
available third-party packaging options (for example, conda-forge).

## About

PathSim is a Python framework for modeling continuous-time, discrete-time,
and hybrid dynamical systems as block diagrams. It targets engineers and
researchers who want a readable, scriptable alternative to traditional
simulation tools without giving up solver depth: more than thirty explicit,
implicit, and adaptive integrators, zero-crossing events and scheduled
triggers, hot-swappable blocks, and hierarchical subsystems. The only
runtime dependencies are numpy, scipy, and matplotlib.

Around the core sits a full ecosystem. PathView provides a visual
block-diagram editor in the browser, FastSim is a Rust engine with the
same API that also generates standalone C for embedded deployment, and
dedicated toolboxes cover chemical, battery, vehicle, flight, and RF
engineering. PathSim and its domain toolboxes are released under the MIT
license.

## Installation

## Ecosystem

pathview

Visual block diagram editor for building and simulating PathSim models in the browser.

fastsim

Fast Rust reimplementation of PathSim with an identical Python API and standalone C code generation for embedded deployment.

pathsim

Build and simulate continuous-time, discrete-time, and hybrid dynamical systems using block diagrams.

chem

Thermodynamic property correlations, activity coefficients, equations of state, and tritium processing.

batt

Battery cell blocks with PyBaMM integration for coupled electrothermal simulation.

vehicle

Tire models, suspension systems, and powertrain components for vehicle dynamics simulation.

flight

Six degrees of freedom equations of motion, aerodynamics, and propulsion for flight simulation.

rf

S-parameter networks, transmission lines, amplifiers, and mixers for RF and microwave simulation.

fmi

Wrap Co-Simulation and Model-Exchange FMUs (FMI 2.0 / 3.0) as PathSim blocks, driven by FMPy.

## Features

Hot-Swappable

Switch blocks and solvers during active simulation at runtime.

MIMO Capable

Multiple input, multiple output ports built into all blocks.

30+ Solvers

Implicit, explicit, and adaptive integrators for stiff and non-stiff systems.

Hierarchical

Nested subsystems for modular, reusable component design.

Event Handling

Zero-crossing detection and scheduled events for hybrid systems.

Extensible

Create custom blocks by subclassing the base Block class.

Browser Editor

Design and simulate visually with PathView using Pyodide.

Domain Toolboxes

Specialized blocks for chemical, vehicle, flight, and RF engineering.

# Go Micro

Go Micro is a Go framework for distributed systems development.

It provides RPC, service discovery, messaging, storage, and configuration.
Agents use services as tools to carry out work.
The gateway exposes services through HTTP and MCP for other applications and agents.
Each component uses a Go interface with a default implementation that can be replaced.

## Features

* **Services:** RPC with streaming, message encoding and service discovery.
* **Agents:** models, conversation history, tools, background tasks, and recovery.

## Getting started

Install the framework:

```
go get go-micro.dev/v6@latest
```

* Build and run a service — Go code and RPC; no model needed.
* Expose services to agents — connect your existing agent through MCP.
* Build a service with an agent — scaffold, run, and chat with your service.
* Chat with services — use Go Micro’s agent from the terminal.

Choose what you need. Chat does not require the gateway.

# OpenWork



OpenWork is the free, open-source alternative to Claude Cowork and Codex: a desktop app for macOS, Windows, and Linux where AI agents do real work on your own files. It is built on OpenCode, works with any model — 50+ providers, your own API keys, or local models via Ollama — and lets teams share skills and MCP servers.

**Download OpenWork** · GitHub releases · Docs

Read this in: 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · 日本語

Add one OpenWork MCP to Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, or another compatible agent and reuse the same skills, MCPs, and connected services across your tools, teammates, and machines. Create something once, share it with coworkers or friends, or keep it for yourself.

The desktop app is there when you want a dedicated workspace, but it is not required. You can use OpenWork from the agent you already have. For larger organizations, the admin interface lets you publish capabilities, manage access, and configure shared or per-user connections.



## Why OpenWork instead of Claude Cowork

* **Free and open source.** The desktop app is MIT-licensed; no OpenWork account is required to use it locally.
* **Any model.** Bring your own API key, sign in with ChatGPT, or run local models through Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible server. See Add a custom LLM.
* **Runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux** as a desktop app — not a CLI.
* **Your files stay local.** Cloud is optional.
* **Share skills and MCP servers with your team.** See Share skills with your team and Shared MCP connections.
* **Self-host** the team control plane on your own infrastructure. See Self-host.
* **Bring your Cowork setup.** Skills, Claude-compatible plugins, and MCP servers carry over. See Migrate from Claude Cowork.

## Install with your AI agent

Already use an AI agent? Copy this prompt and paste it into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ChatGPT, or any agent that can run commands on your computer.

```
Install OpenWork on my computer, set up my first workspace, and open it ready to use. Follow the steps in https://openworklabs.com/start.md?v=hero
```

1. Installs OpenWork
2. Creates your workspace
3. Opens it ready to run

## Use OpenWork from any agent

The OpenWork MCP brings your assigned skills, plugins, MCP connections, Google Workspace, and Microsoft 365 capabilities into any compatible agent.

It exposes four tools: `search_capabilities` finds what you can use, `execute_capability` runs it, and `list_skills` / `get_skill` list your skills and read one SKILL.md directly. After adding the MCP, your client opens a browser so you can sign in and choose your OpenWork organization.

### Codex

```
codex mcp add openwork --url https://api.openworklabs.com/mcp/agent
```

### Claude Code

```
claude mcp add --transport http openwork https://api.openworklabs.com/mcp/agent
```

d up to be easy to use—whether you're new or
experienced, working on brand new projects alone, or large scale software
projects with large histories and teams.

Jujutsu is unlike most other systems, because internally it abstracts the user
interface and version control algorithms from the *storage systems* used to
serve your content. This allows it to serve as a VCS with many possible physical
backends, that may have their own data or networking models—like Mercurial or Breezy, or hybrid systems like Google's cloud-based design, Piper/CitC.

Today, we use Git repositories as a storage layer to serve and track content,
making it **compatible with many of your favorite Git-based tools, right now!** However, note that only commits and files are stored in Git; bookmarks
(branches) and other higher-level metadata are stored in custom storage outside
of Git. All core developers use Jujutsu to develop Jujutsu, right here on
GitHub. But it should hopefully work with your favorite Git forges, too.

We combine many distinct design choices and concepts from other version control
systems into a single tool. Some of those sources of inspiration include:

* **Git**: We make an effort to be fast—with a snappy UX, efficient
    algorithms, correct data structures, and good-old-fashioned attention to
    detail. The default storage backend uses Git repositories for "physical
    storage", for wide interoperability and ease of onboarding.

* **Mercurial & Sapling**: There are many Mercurial-inspired features, such as
    the revset language to select commits. There is no explicit index or staging area. Branches are "anonymous" like Mercurial, so you don't need
    to make up a name for each small change. Primitives for rewriting history are
    powerful and simple. Formatting output is done with a robust template language
    that can be configured by the user.

* **Darcs**: Jujutsu keeps track of conflicts as first-class objects in its model; they are first-class in the same way commits
    are, while alternatives like Git simply think of conflicts as textual diffs.
    While not as rigorous as systems like Darcs (which is based on a formalized
    theory of patches, as opposed to snapshots), the effect is that many forms of
    conflict resolution can be performed and propagated automatically.

And it adds several innovative, useful features of its own:

* **Working-copy-as-a-commit**: Changes to files are recorded automatically as normal commits, and amended on every subsequent change. This "snapshot"
    design simplifies the user-facing data model (commits are the only visible
    object), simplifies internal algorithms, and completely subsumes features like
    Git's stashes or the index/staging-area.

* **Operation log & undo**: Jujutsu records every operation that is performed on the
    repository, from commits, to pulls, to pushes. This makes debugging problems like
    "what just happened?" or "how did I end up here?" easier, *especially* when
    you're helping your coworker answer those questions about their repository!
    And because everything is recorded, you can undo that mistake you just made
    with ease. Version control has finally entered the 1960s!

* **Automatic rebase and conflict resolution**: When you modify a commit, every
    descendent is automatically rebased on top of the freshly-modified one. This
    makes "patch-based" workflows a breeze. If you resolve a conflict in a commit,
    the *resolution* of that conflict is also propagated through descendants as
    well. In effect, this is a completely transparent version of `git rebase --update-refs` combined with `git rerere`, supported by design.

The following features are available for use, but experimental; they may have
bugs, backwards incompatible storage changes, and user-interface changes!

* **Safe, concurrent replication**: Have you ever wanted to store your version
    controlled repositories inside a Dropbox folder? Or continuously backup
    repositories to S3? No? Well, now you can!

    The fundamental problem with using filesystems like Dropbox and backup tools
    like `rsync` on your typical Git/Mercurial repositories is that they rely
    on *local filesystem operations* being atomic, serialized, and non-concurrent
    with respect to other reads and writes—which is *not* true when operating on
    distributed file systems, or when operations like concurrent file copies (for
    backup) happen while lock files are being held.

    Jujutsu is instead designed to be safe under concurrent scenarios;
    simply using rsync or Dropbox and then using that resulting repository
    should never result in a repository in a *corrupt state*. The worst that *should* happen is that it will expose conflicts between the local and remote
    state, leaving you to resolve them.

Skill directory: /workspace/.skills/scientific-writing

# Scientific Writing

A report PDF is produced by compiling the Edison LaTeX template.

## 1. LaTeX setup

First, create a clean latex working directory, such as `latex_report/`.

Then, make two calls to fetch template latex files and build a bibliography.

### Download template files

```python
from e14c.reports.latex import fetch_edison_template

fetch_edison_template("latex_report")
```

This places the following in `latex_report/`:

- `template.tex` - loads arxiv package, additional default Edison styles, and document structure. Rename this to something more descriptive
- `arxiv.sty`
- `references.bib` - placeholder
- `edison-logo.pdf` - logo for the cover page (already configured in the template)

### House style lock

`template.tex` is a complete report with the house style already wired in - cover page, logo, colour palette, callout boxes, and the Data Sources table. Rename it, then fill it in: replace the `[REPLACE]` placeholders with your content and leave the `[KEEP]` blocks alone.

Compile that renamed copy as is - the preamble stays as fetched, the `[KEEP]` blocks stay where they are, and `arxiv.sty` is never edited. Fill the `[REPLACE]` placeholders and add sections between them; do not rebuild the document body around a cover page of your own. Depart from the house style only when the task explicitly says not to use the Edison template; adjectives like polished or demo-quality are not an opt-out.

If compile errors are in your content, fix the content. If they are in the template or `arxiv.sty`, report them; do not replace the template to get a clean compile.

### Build the bibliography

Build `latex_report/references.bib` as described in the `bibliography` skill. Load that skill first if it is not already loaded. It merges the literature task citations and the saved literature and web citation files into one file. The template's `\printbibliography` renders it.

Note: this overwrites anything in `references.bib`.

## 2. Drafting

### Skeleton

The orchestrator agent may have provided an outline of structural elements for the main text. Try to adhere to those. If the outline is ambiguous, here is an example

```
 1. Cover page
 2. Abstract / Executive Summary: one page max.
 3. Table of contents: long reports only (>= 10 pages). Omit for shorter reports.
 4. Introduction / Context: what is known, what the gap is.
 5. Methodology: reference trajectory/tasks as needed.
 6. Main content sections: organized by research question
 7. Recommendations (if needed): tiered near-, medium-, long-term
 8. Discussion / Caveats / Limitations: standalone or per-recommendation
 9. Conclusion: brief synthesis
10. Output provenance table: every asset to a real task UUID with a chat_url link
11. Bibliography: generated from references.bib via biblatex
```

## 3. Paper elements

Read the fetched template before drafting and reuse its approved patterns.

### Literature citations

Cite in-line using `\citep{key}`, or for multiple citations, `\citep{key1,key2}`. The template's `biblatex` (numbered style) handles rendering as `[N]` and truncates long author lists to the first 6 + "et al.".

The `template.tex` contains a command to render the bibliography.

### Edison trajectory citations

Any outputs of tasks (especially analyses tasks) that appear in the paper should be properly referenced to allow the reader to trace back to the originating trajectory. Ideal places to include these references include:

- The end of a figure/table legend
- Within a methods section
- Within a results section

Sub-agent outputs use the sub-agent's UUID, passed in via the dispatch. Outputs you produced yourself use `os.environ["TRAJECTORY_ID"]`. Never use `ORCHESTRATOR` or any placeholder string.

`\edtraj{<url>}{<short>}` renders `Edison: <short>` for inline trajectory references. Trajectory URLs should be obtained programmatically to reduce errors as follows:

```python
from e14c.subagents import chat_url

sub_url = chat_url("74d1ef6b-0f34-4805-ba2b-c110086e7e93")  # task (default)
self_url = chat_url()  # this trajectory
artifact_url = chat_url("report-pdf-ab12", kind="data_entry")  # uploaded artifact
```

For artifacts, wrap with href:

```latex
\href{<artifact_url>}{data\_entry:report-pdf-ab12}
```

See the template for how to update the Edison Platform Data Sources table.

### Tables and statistics

- Booktabs and alternating row shading on tables where it aids readability.
- Color-code priority programs.
- P-values appear alongside ORs/betas. No naked effect sizes. For discovery analyses, show only FDR-significant results.

### Figures

One overview figure per report.

- `e14c.image_generation.generate_image` for label-heavy scientific figures.
- `e14c.image_generation.generate_infographic` for non-text-heavy conceptual overviews.

You may also pass a reference image to edit.

Visual style: white or light background, muted palette (navy/black/gray), Nature-style, publication-ready. No chartjunk, no cartoon styling, no decoration. Every figure caption ends with the producing task UUID, hyperlinked via `chat_url` (see Edison trajectory citations above).

## 4. Pre-delivery validation

Complete the applicable checks before calling `submit_answer`.

### Build

- [ ] Compile the actual main `.tex` file with `tectonic`. Resolve compilation errors, undefined references, and alignment errors.
- [ ] Unless the task opted out of the house style, confirm the compiled file is the renamed template: the preamble differs from the fetched `template.tex` only by `[REPLACE]` substitutions, the `[KEEP]` blocks and the template cover page are intact, and `arxiv.sty` is unchanged. A hand-written preamble that loads `arxiv`, or a self-authored `titlepage` in place of the template cover, does not qualify.
- [ ] Confirm every `\citep{key}` resolves to an entry in `references.bib`.
- [ ] Include a table of contents only when the final PDF is at least 10 pages.
- [ ] Place `\FloatBarrier` or `\clearpage` before References so figures and tables cannot drift beyond it.

### Content and provenance

- [ ] Check every quantitative claim against the originating task output.
- [ ] Sweep the draft for claims with no citation. For each, either attach the source or restate it as explicit inference.
- [ ] Confirm figure and table captions, numbering, and in-text references agree.
- [ ] Ensure repeated values, ranked lists, scores, and entity sets are consistent across sections.
- [ ] Associate every task-derived asset with its originating task UUID and `chat_url`.
- [ ] Wrap artifact references using `chat_url(<id>, kind="data_entry")`.
- [ ] Upload every supporting file named for the reader and reference it with a `data_entry:` URI.
- [ ] Remove placeholders, draft or version labels, prior-iteration language, and inaccessible internal paths.
- [ ] Remove meta-context, including mentions of prompts, system internals, the orchestrator, or the document-generation process.

### Layout

- [ ] For new documents or changes that can affect layout, use `explore` to inspect every rendered PDF page for overflowing tables, clipped figures, misplaced floats, orphaned headings, blank pages, and excessive whitespace.
- [ ] For a targeted layout fix, inspect the affected pages again. Skip full layout inspection only for minor text edits unlikely to change pagination.

Run each applicable check once. If one fails, fix the issue and rerun only the affected checks. Submit when all applicable checks pass.

# Status: Moving Towards PCB!

We're beginning to layout the components and finalize the design of our quantum computer! As we continue to design the PCB, we are also working with optical engineers to make our logic gates more compact which will enable us to shrink the design even further than we already have!

To speed up R&D, we've decided to replace the ARM CPU with a QSeven2.0 spec'd "computer on module". There are a variety of benefits to doing this, one major benefit being that we can switch between a variety of x86 and ARM processors.

== brainlife https://brainlife.io/docs/
Anyone can develop, use, combine, and reuse Apps to build complex pipelines for customized brain data analyses on the platform. You can publish apps to be used privately or shared publicly with the brainlife.io community. Combining multiple Apps allows for high-throughput data processing and aggregation across thousands of datasets.
The best way to manage your data is with brainlife.io’s Projects feature. Here you can organize your datasets, perform data processing, and share results with your team by granting varying levels of access to members of your group. Projects can be public or private.
brainlife Datatypes are maintained by individual developers and are updated at [brainlife.io](https://brainlife.io/datatypes).
Our compute resources are unique because, instead of running an entire workflow on a single resource, App developers can identify the best resource for each individual App by scoring brainlife.io’s compute resources on how well they work with each App. brainlife.io automatically keeps track of success rate and time to compute so that users can easily see how efficiently each resource processes data for each App.
Users can perform data visualizations on brainlife.io in the cloud instead of on their own computer, which means better security and data management. Data visualization gives users feedback on the quality of the results generated by Apps and pipelines. The visualizations allow users to run popular software for data visualization like FreeView, FSLview, or MRview. Users can additionally run GPU-rendered visualizations on the cloud through Docker and VNC. Similar to Apps, developers can contribute visualizations to the platform.

# K-Dense BYOK

          

> ### 🎥 Webinar recording: **Getting Started with K-Dense BYOK**
> 
> An online walkthrough of installing Kady and running your first research task, with live Q&A.
> 
> 👉 **Watch the recording on YouTube**

**Your own AI research assistant, running on your computer, powered by the accounts and API keys you choose.**

   

K-Dense BYOK (Bring Your Own Keys) is a free, open-source app that gives you **Kady** — an AI research assistant for scientists in any field. Describe a task in plain language — *analyze this dataset*, *review my manuscript*, *search the literature*, *build this figure* — and Kady works through it in a complete research workspace. It can inspect your files, write and run analysis code, search and read sources, create figures and reports, and keep a living record of what it did.

Four things to know up front:

* **No coding experience required.** You describe what you want; Kady writes and runs the code and shows you its progress as it works.
* **Every step is on the record.** Kady keeps a lab notebook of its reasoning and a separate, automatically recorded log of what actually ran and which files each step produced, so results can be checked, traced, and reproduced.
* **Your workspace stays on your computer.** Projects, conversations, notebooks, and results live in ordinary folders on your machine; K-Dense does not host or store them. When you use a hosted AI model, the material needed for that request is sent directly to the provider you selected under that provider's privacy terms. Use a local Ollama model when data must not leave your machine.
* **The app itself is free; provider charges and limits remain yours.** Use prepaid OpenRouter, connect a supported AI subscription, or run free local models. Kady tracks paid OpenRouter usage and Anthropic OAuth's documented metered extra usage against project spending caps. ChatGPT, Copilot, xAI, Kimi Code, and Meta Muse subscription usage is tracked separately because those providers manage quotas and overages; a subscription login does not imply unlimited or free usage.

> **Beta:** K-Dense BYOK is currently in beta. Many features and improvements are on the way. Star us on GitHub to stay in the loop, and follow K-Dense on X, LinkedIn, YouTube, and Reddit for release notes and tutorials.

> 🎬 **Prefer to watch first?** The Future of Research is Open: Introducing K-Dense BYOK walks through what the app does and how to get set up. More walkthroughs in Tutorial videos.

> 📄 **Read the paper:** K-Dense BYOK: An Open-Source AI Research Assistant That Runs Locally and Keeps a Hash-Chained Lab Notebook (arXiv:2610.00074). If you use K-Dense BYOK in your research, please cite it.

## CompBioBench

As of September 11, 2026, K-Dense BYOK holds **\#2** on the public CompBioBench v1 leaderboard.

CompBioBench is a Genentech benchmark of 100 computational-biology tasks. Each task has one exact-match answer. The gold answers stay on the leaderboard, so an independent grader scores every run.

We ran the same K-Dense BYOK harness four times through OpenRouter. Each run used one model and one isolated project per question.


Ranks will move as new submissions arrive. For agreement, failures, and cost on the first three runs, see K-Dense BYOK on CompBioBench.

The benchmark was designed, run, and evaluated internally by K-Dense rather than an independent third party, so the results should be interpreted as an internal evaluation under the tested setup, not as a universal measure of platform performance.

# T3 Code

The open-source control plane for coding agents.

**Download** · iOS · Android · Web · Docs · Discord



T3 Code runs the coding agents on your machine and gives them one fast interface. Start a thread at your desk, then approve the next step from your phone.

It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build, Antigravity, Kiro, Pi, Muse Code, fx, and any ACP agent. If an agent is set up on your computer, T3 Code can control it.

## What you get

* **Your subscriptions.** T3 Code does not resell tokens. It drives the agents you are already signed in to.
* **Every agent in one place.** Change models in the middle of a thread. Let Claude hand a task to Codex.
* **Desktop, web, and phone.** One server, and every client shows the same threads. There are apps for iOS and Android.
* **Remote ready.** Run agents on any machine. Connect over your local network, Tailscale, or T3 Connect.
* **Git built in.** Each thread can work in its own worktree. Review the diff, then commit, push, and open a pull request with one button.
* **Fast.** Performance is a feature here. We measure it, and we treat a dropped frame as a bug.
* **Open.** Source code is MIT licensed. If you don't like something, fork it under your own branding (see Trademarks and forks).

## Install

### Desktop app

Download T3 Code for macOS, Windows, or Linux. You can also use a package manager:


### Command line

This installs the `t3` command. Run `t3` to start the server and open the web app.

```
curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```
irm https://t3.codes/install.ps1 | iex
```

To try it once without an install, run `npx t3@latest`.

### Phone

Get the app from the App Store or Google Play. Then follow remote access to connect it to your computer.

### Sign in to an agent

T3 Code needs one agent that is installed and signed in. For example, install Claude Code and run `claude auth login`, or install Codex CLI and run `codex login`.

Provider setup has the steps for each agent. Install T3 Code covers nightly builds, AppImage, WSL, and NixOS.

## "Wait, what are you selling me?"

Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork the source code and build the tool that you want, under your own name and branding.

## Documentation

* Install and first run
* Remote access from a phone or another machine
* Permission modes
* Source control
* Connect outside agents over MCP
* FAQ

All docs has the full list.

## Contributing

We have limited review capacity. Small, focused fixes are the most likely to be merged. Features need an approved discussion first.

* Read CONTRIBUTING.md before you report a bug or open a pull request.
* Put feature requests in Ideas.
* Build from source with the development runbook. The architecture overview explains how it works.
* Get help in Discord.

## Trademarks and forks

The MIT license applies **only to the source code**. It does not grant any rights to T3 Tools, Inc.'s trademarks, branding, or trade dress, including the **T3 Code** name, wordmark, logos, and application icons.

If you fork, redistribute, or build on T3 Code's source code:

* **Use your own branding.** Replace the T3 Code name, wordmark, logos, and application icons in any public fork, redistributed build, website, package, or app store listing.
* **Be explicitly clear that your project is unofficial.** Do not use the T3 Code name, wordmark, logo, or branding in your own projects without making it unmistakably clear that your project is unofficial and not affiliated with or endorsed by T3 Tools, Inc.

Using our name, wordmark, logo, or branding in a way that suggests official status or affiliation is trademark infringement and unlawful. **Any project indicating or implying that it is an official version of T3 Code when it is not will be pursued to the full extent of the law.**

I wrote **[owner_class_audit.csv](/workspace/owner_class_audit.csv)** with all **120 accounts**, in input order, using exactly the seven requested columns. I checked a primary website or repository for every account and did not use financial outcomes to choose classes.

| Class | Count |
|---|---:|

| **Total** | **120** |

I marked **36 judgment calls**. [Review notes](/workspace/owner_class_audit_notes.md) explain every flagged account, with source links and limitations. These are unweighted sample counts, not population estimates.

### Hardest classifications

- **`Spooky-Manufacturing` → core:** Its manufacturer description and computer designs suggest a product-focused hardware developer, but legal-entity and paid-offering evidence remain incomplete.
- **`OpenMontageInc` → core:** The repository links to its Studio product; treating it as a commercial project company requires inference because a paid tier was not established.
- **`labmlai` → community:** The checked pages establish open tutorials and self-hosted tools, but not an owning company or paid offering.
- **`micro` → core:** The hosted assistant and open framework suggest one product ecosystem, but their precise commercial relationship is insufficiently explicit.
- **`K-Dense-AI` → complement:** I distinguish its free skills/local assistant from its paid hosted agents. Whether these constitute variants of the same project is genuinely debatable.
- **`Textualize` → complement:** Its current homepage presents separate writing applications alongside the framework; I did not establish a current paid framework edition.
- **`php` → community:** A supporting foundation does not, by itself, establish ownership or control of the PHP organization account.
- **`spacetelescope` → academic:** I apply the research-institute rule to the AURA-operated institute; operating NASA missions does not make it a government agency.
- **`mixOmics-org` → academic:** I interpret the stated University of Melbourne lab leadership as an academic account, despite worldwide contributors.

### Analytical decisions

- I distinguished ownership and stewardship from contributor employment, sponsorship, and fiscal hosting.
- I applied the maintainer-company tie-breaker and flagged borderline product relationships rather than treating every project-branded account as community-owned.
- Where ownership was identifiable but the class remained uncertain, I chose the more likely class and set `judgment=1`. **Zero unknowns does not mean every account’s legal ownership was conclusively verified.**

outputs.text:
# Classifying the GitHub organizations that own popular repositories

Part of a pre-registered study (issue #380): who owns the most-starred open-source repositories, and (later, in a
separate step) what those owners earn and raise. Your job is ONLY the first step: identify and classify each owner.

**Do not look up, record or use any financial outcome** (funding, valuation, revenue, IPO, acquisition price,
shutdown) when deciding a class. The class must not depend on whether the owner succeeded. You may note an
acquisition or shutdown in `status_hint` only if you happen to know it, but never let it change the class.

## Input

A CSV with one row per GitHub organization account: `owner` (the GitHub login), rank by stars, frames (A = among
the 2,000 most-starred repos on GitHub; B = among the most-starred repos in science topics), number of repos,
total stars, the account's name, website (`blog`), e-mail domain, location, creation year, Wikidata item if one
lists this GitHub username, description, and up to three top repositories with stars, language and description.

## Classes (exactly one per owner)

| cls | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `core` | A company whose main paid product is the project itself in another form: a hosted/cloud service of it, an open-core or enterprise edition, paid licences or support for it, or hardware it sells. Examples: Elastic (`elastic`), Grafana Labs, Supabase, HashiCorp (even though IBM now owns it), Docker Inc. (`docker`, `moby`), Vercel (Next.js; hosting platform marketed to its users), Hugging Face (Hub), Ollama, n8n, LangChain, Opentrons (sells the robots), Prusa Research, Ultralytics (paid licences), DeepSeek (sells API access to its open-weight models) |
| `complement` | A company that publishes the project but earns most of its revenue from other products. Examples: Microsoft, Google/Alphabet (`google`, `tensorflow`, `angular`, `flutter`, `golang`, `google-research`, `puppeteer`), Meta (`facebookresearch`, `meta-llama`), Alibaba (`alibaba`, `ant-design`, `agentscope-ai`), Baidu (`PaddlePaddle`), ByteDance, Tencent, Airbnb, X/Twitter, Cloudflare, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Red Hat/IBM for `ansible`, Broadcom for `spring-projects`, Shopify for `remix-run`, Genymobile for `scrcpy` (sells Genymotion), a consultancy publishing a side tool, a company whose open repo is a list or SDK for a closed product |
| `nonprofit` | A foundation or other nonprofit that owns or stewards the project: Apache Software Foundation, Linux Foundation and its sub-foundations (CNCF for `kubernetes`, OpenJS for `nodejs` and `electron`, PyTorch Foundation for `pytorch` and `vllm-project`, Agentic AI Foundation for `modelcontextprotocol`), Python Software Foundation (`python`, `psf`), Django Software Foundation, Rust Foundation (`rust-lang`), Mozilla, freeCodeCamp, Free Ebook Foundation, Godot Foundation, Open Home Foundation (`home-assistant`), NumFOCUS-sponsored projects ONLY if NumFOCUS or another foundation is the legal home rather than a mere fiscal sponsor (otherwise `community`) |
| `academic` | A university, a university lab or group, or an academic research institute (including state-funded research institutes such as Shanghai AI Laboratory, Max Planck, EMBL, Broad Institute, HHMI Janelia, Allen Institute). Examples: `HKUDS` (HKU), `CompVis` (LMU Munich) |
| `government` | A government agency, national laboratory or government-owned body: `NationalSecurityAgency`, NASA, NIST, NIH/NCBI, DOE national labs (LLNL, ORNL, NREL, Sandia, ...), CERN, UK GDS (`alphagov`) |
| `community` | A project with no owning legal entity, or one that only uses a fiscal host (Open Collective, Open Source Collective, Software Freedom Conservancy, NumFOCUS fiscal sponsorship, Commons Conservancy). Examples: `vuejs`, `twbs` (Bootstrap), `yt-dlp`, `ohmyzsh`, `neovim`, `Homebrew`, `bitcoin`, `TheAlgorithms`, `public-apis`, `d3`, `axios`, `obsproject`, `pallets`, `numpy`, `scipy`, `pandas-dev`, `matplotlib`, scientific-software collaborations without a single owning institution |
| `unknown` | Not identifiable from public sources after a reasonable check |

Tie-breakers:
- Classify the **organization account**, by who owns or controls it today. If a company bought the project's
  company, the class stays `core` and `parent` names the buyer (HashiCorp → `core`, parent IBM).
- Company vs. project org: if a GitHub org is the project's home and a company founded by the maintainers sells a
  hosted or enterprise version (e.g. `mermaid-js` → Mermaid Chart; `storybookjs` → Chromatic), use `core`, set
  `judgment=1` and name the company in `entity`.
- An AI lab that releases open weights and sells API access to those same models → `core` (judgment=1). An AI lab
  whose open repos are tools around closed models → `complement`.
- Academic spin-out companies are companies (`core` or `complement`), not `academic`.
- Crypto/blockchain: classify the developing company or foundation as usual, and set `crypto=1`.
- A one-person "org" that is clearly just an individual's projects → `community` (note "individual's org").
- Content repositories (lists, books, courses) are still classified by owner.
- If you're unsure between two classes, pick the more likely one and set `judgment=1`. Use `unknown` only if you
  can't identify the owner at all.

## How to check

Use your own knowledge first. For any owner you're not sure about (new 2025–26 projects especially), check the
organization's website (the `blog` field) or the repository README with WebFetch (e.g.
`https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>` or the website's about/pricing page) to see whether a company sells something.
A pricing page, "Enterprise", "Cloud" or "Sign up" with paid tiers is evidence of `core` or `complement`. Spend at
most a couple of fetches per owner. Do not use web search for financial information.

## Output

Write a CSV (with a header) to the path given in your task, one row per input owner, in input order, no rows
skipped, with these columns:

`owner,cls,entity,parent,country,basis,judgment,crypto,status_hint,source_url`

- `entity`: the owning organization's common or legal name (e.g. "Grafana Labs", "University of Hong Kong",
  "Python Software Foundation"). For `community`, the project name.
- `parent`: ultimate parent company or institution if different (e.g. "Alphabet", "IBM", "Linux Foundation").
- `country`: ISO-2 country code of the owning entity's headquarters if known (US, CN, DE, ...), else blank.
- `basis`: at most 15 words: what the class rests on (e.g. "sells Grafana Cloud and Enterprise", "HKU data science lab").
- `judgment`: 1 if a judgment call, else 0. `crypto`: 1 or 0.
- `status_hint`: optional, e.g. "acquired by IBM 2025", "subsidiary", "archived".
- `source_url`: the page you checked, or blank if from knowledge.

Quote fields containing commas. When done, reply with: the number of rows written, counts by class, and a list of
the owners you marked `unknown` or `judgment=1` with a few words on why.

print(x.shape)
print(x.columns.tolist())
print(x[['owner','name','blog','description']].to_string(index=True))

outputs.name: stdout
outputs.text:
# Classifying the GitHub organizations that own popular repositories

Part of a pre-registered study (issue #380): who owns the most-starred open-source repositories, and (later, in a
separate step) what those owners earn and raise. Your job is ONLY the first step: identify and classify each owner.

**Do not look up, record or use any financial outcome** (funding, valuation, revenue, IPO, acquisition price,
shutdown) when deciding a class. The class must not depend on whether the owner succeeded. You may note an
acquisition or shutdown in `status_hint` only if you happen to know it, but never let it change the class.

## Input

A CSV with one row per GitHub organization account: `owner` (the GitHub login), rank by stars, frames (A = among
the 2,000 most-starred repos on GitHub; B = among the most-starred repos in science topics), number of repos,
total stars, the account's name, website (`blog`), e-mail domain, location, creation year, Wikidata item if one
lists this GitHub username, description, and up to three top repositories with stars, language and description.

## Classes (exactly one per owner)

| cls | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `core` | A company whose main paid product is the project itself in another form: a hosted/cloud service of it, an open-core or enterprise edition, paid licences or support for it, or hardware it sells. Examples: Elastic (`elastic`), Grafana Labs, Supabase, HashiCorp (even though IBM now owns it), Docker Inc. (`docker`, `moby`), Vercel (Next.js; hosting platform marketed to its users), Hugging Face (Hub), Ollama, n8n, LangChain, Opentrons (sells the robots), Prusa Research, Ultralytics (paid licences), DeepSeek (sells API access to its open-weight models) |
| `complement` | A company that publishes the project but earns most of its revenue from other products. Examples: Microsoft, Google/Alphabet (`google`, `tensorflow`, `angular`, `flutter`, `golang`, `google-research`, `puppeteer`), Meta (`facebookresearch`, `meta-llama`), Alibaba (`alibaba`, `ant-design`, `agentscope-ai`), Baidu (`PaddlePaddle`), ByteDance, Tencent, Airbnb, X/Twitter, Cloudflare, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Red Hat/IBM for `ansible`, Broadcom for `spring-projects`, Shopify for `remix-run`, Genymobile for `scrcpy` (sells Genymotion), a consultancy publishing a side tool, a company whose open repo is a list or SDK for a closed product |
| `nonprofit` | A foundation or other nonprofit that owns or stewards the project: Apache Software Foundation, Linux Foundation and its sub-foundations (CNCF for `kubernetes`, OpenJS for `nodejs` and `electron`, PyTorch Foundation for `pytorch` and `vllm-project`, Agentic AI Foundation for `modelcontextprotocol`), Python Software Foundation (`python`, `psf`), Django Software Foundation, Rust Foundation (`rust-lang`), Mozilla, freeCodeCamp, Free Ebook Foundation, Godot Foundation, Open Home Foundation (`home-assistant`), NumFOCUS-sponsored projects ONLY if NumFOCUS or another foundation is the legal home rather than a mere fiscal sponsor (otherwise `community`) |
| `academic` | A university, a university lab or group, or an academic research institute (including state-funded research institutes such as Shanghai AI Laboratory, Max Planck, EMBL, Broad Institute, HHMI Janelia, Allen Institute). Examples: `HKUDS` (HKU), `CompVis` (LMU Munich) |
| `government` | A government agency, national laboratory or government-owned body: `NationalSecurityAgency`, NASA, NIST, NIH/NCBI, DOE national labs (LLNL, ORNL, NREL, Sandia, ...), CERN, UK GDS (`alphagov`) |
| `community` | A project with no owning legal entity, or one that only uses a fiscal host (Open Collective, Open Source Collective, Software Freedom Conservancy, NumFOCUS fiscal sponsorship, Commons Conservancy). Examples: `vuejs`, `twbs` (Bootstrap), `yt-dlp`, `ohmyzsh`, `neovim`, `Homebrew`, `bitcoin`, `TheAlgorithms`, `public-apis`, `d3`, `axios`, `obsproject`, `pallets`, `numpy`, `scipy`, `pandas-dev`, `matplotlib`, scientific-software collaborations without a single owning institution |
| `unknown` | Not identifiable from public sources after a reasonable check |

Tie-breakers:
- Classify the **organization account**, by who owns or controls it today. If a company bought the project's
  company, the class stays `core` and `parent` names the buyer (HashiCorp → `core`, parent IBM).
- Company vs. project org: if a GitHub org is the project's home and a company founded by the maintainers sells a
  hosted or enterprise version (e.g. `mermaid-js` → Mermaid Chart; `storybookjs` → Chromatic), use `core`, set
  `judgment=1` and name the company in `entity`.
- An AI lab that releases open weights and sells API access to those same models → `core` (judgment=1). An AI lab
  whose open repos are tools around closed models → `complement`.
- Academic spin-out companies are companies (`core` or `complement`), not `academic`.
- Crypto/blockchain: classify the developing company or foundation as usual, and set `crypto=1`.
- A one-person "org" that is clearly just an individual's projects → `community` (note "individual's org").
- Content repositories (lists, books, courses) are still classified by owner.
- If you're unsure between two classes, pick the more likely one and set `judgment=1`. Use `unknown` only if you
  can't identify the owner at all.

## How to check

Use your own knowledge first. For any owner you're not sure about (new 2025–26 projects especially), check the
organization's website (the `blog` field) or the repository README with WebFetch (e.g.
`https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>` or the website's about/pricing page) to see whether a company sells something.
A pricing page, "Enterprise", "Cloud" or "Sign up" with paid tiers is evidence of `core` or `complement`. Spend at
most a couple of fetches per owner. Do not use web search for financial information.

## Output

Write a CSV (with a header) to the path given in your task, one row per input owner, in input order, no rows
skipped, with these columns:

`owner,cls,entity,parent,country,basis,judgment,crypto,status_hint,source_url`

- `entity`: the owning organization's common or legal name (e.g. "Grafana Labs", "University of Hong Kong",
  "Python Software Foundation"). For `community`, the project name.
- `parent`: ultimate parent company or institution if different (e.g. "Alphabet", "IBM", "Linux Foundation").
- `country`: ISO-2 country code of the owning entity's headquarters if known (US, CN, DE, ...), else blank.
- `basis`: at most 15 words: what the class rests on (e.g. "sells Grafana Cloud and Enterprise", "HKU data science lab").
- `judgment`: 1 if a judgment call, else 0. `crypto`: 1 or 0.
- `status_hint`: optional, e.g. "acquired by IBM 2025", "subsidiary", "archived".
- `source_url`: the page you checked, or blank if from knowledge.

Quote fields containing commas. When done, reply with: the number of rows written, counts by class, and a list of
the owners you marked `unknown` or `judgment=1` with a few words on why.

outputs.text:
- A one-person "org" that is clearly just an individual's projects → `community` (note "individual's org").
- Content repositories (lists, books, courses) are still classified by owner.
- If you're unsure between two classes, pick the more likely one and set `judgment=1`. Use `unknown` only if you
  can't identify the owner at all.

## How to check

Use your own knowledge first. For any owner you're not sure about (new 2025–26 projects especially), check the
organization's website (the `blog` field) or the repository README with WebFetch (e.g.
`https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>` or the website's about/pricing page) to see whether a company sells something.
A pricing page, "Enterprise", "Cloud" or "Sign up" with paid tiers is evidence of `core` or `complement`. Spend at
most a couple of fetches per owner. Do not use web search for financial information.

## Output

Write a CSV (with a header) to the path given in your task, one row per input owner, in input order, no rows
skipped, with these columns:

`owner,cls,entity,parent,country,basis,judgment,crypto,status_hint,source_url`

- `entity`: the owning organization's common or legal name (e.g. "Grafana Labs", "University of Hong Kong",
  "Python Software Foundation"). For `community`, the project name.
- `parent`: ultimate parent company or institution if different (e.g. "Alphabet", "IBM", "Linux Foundation").
- `country`: ISO-2 country code of the owning entity's headquarters if known (US, CN, DE, ...), else blank.
- `basis`: at most 15 words: what the class rests on (e.g. "sells Grafana Cloud and Enterprise", "HKU data science lab").
- `judgment`: 1 if a judgment call, else 0. `crypto`: 1 or 0.
- `status_hint`: optional, e.g. "acquired by IBM 2025", "subsidiary", "archived".
- `source_url`: the page you checked, or blank if from knowledge.

Quote fields containing commas. When done, reply with: the number of rows written, counts by class, and a list of
the owners you marked `unknown` or `judgment=1` with a few words on why.

evidence={}
citation_paths=set()
def clean_content(text):
    # Exclude incidental outcome-bearing lines; they are never evidence for this audit.
    excluded=re.compile(r'\b(funding|fundrais\w*|valuation|revenue|acquisition price|shutdown|shut down|IPO|raised \$|raised €|series [a-f]\b|seed round)\b',re.I)
    return '\n'.join(line for line in str(text).splitlines() if not excluded.search(line))
def cite_page(key,url,text,author):
    headings=re.findall(r'^#+\s+(.+)$',text,re.M)
    first=next((s.strip() for s in text.splitlines() if s.strip()),key)
    title=(headings[0] if headings else first)[:220]
    title=re.sub(r'!?\[([^]]*)\]\([^)]*\)',r'\1',title)
    def esc(s):
        return str(s).replace('\\','').replace('{','').replace('}','').replace('&',r'\&').replace('_',r'\_').replace('%',r'\%').replace('#',r'\#')
    ck=re.sub('[^A-Za-z0-9]','',key)+'2026source'+str(len(evidence)+1)
    bib='@online{'+ck+',\n  author = {{'+esc(author)+'}},\n  title = {'+esc(title)+'},\n  url = {'+url+'},\n  urldate = {'+str(datetime.date.today())+'}\n}\n'
    citation_paths.add(str(save_citation(bib)))
    return ck
async def check(key,url,author=None,limit=10500):
    try:
        raw=await fetch_parsed_page(url)
        safe=clean_content(raw)
        ck=cite_page(key,url,safe,author or key)
        evidence.setdefault(key,[]).append({'url':url,'text':safe,'citation_key':ck})
        return key,safe[:limit]
    except Exception as e:
        return key,'FETCH FAILED: '+str(e)[:200]
# Preserve and cite first page already checked.

ck=cite_page('anomalyco','https://anoma.ly',safe,'Anomaly')

# What will You Build?

Intent-driven exchanges

Leverage Fuel’s unique spending condition architecture to enable lightweight intent-driven designs.

Real-time prediction markets

Build complex streaming based real-time market designs with Fuel's 1 second block time.

Capital markets/DEXs

Use Fuel's inherent UTXO based asset model to design complex capital markets and DEXs at native levels.

AMMs without Smart Contracts

Combine spending conditions with native assets to build AMMs without smart contracts.

How it works

## One map of the code

One graph across every repository and team, built once and kept current. Nobody re-learns the codebase by hand, and what one engagement learns carries into the next.

---

## Answers with proof

Every answer is a path through the graph you can open, spanning code, docs, wikis and contracts. Evidence rather than opinion, for audited and regulated work.

---

## See what breaks

Before the merge, the graph follows every edge to what a change breaks. The agent reads the graph instead of the repo, so the token bill buys answers.

## Six tools, one binary. Adopt one, or all of them.

bun install and bun test drop into existing Node.js projects. No runtime switch required.

* [bun run](https://bun.com/#tool-run)
* [bun install](https://bun.com/#tool-install)
* [bun test](https://bun.com/#tool-test)
* [bun build](https://bun.com/#tool-build)
* [bun check](https://bun.com/#tool-check)
* [bun fmt](https://bun.com/#tool-fmt)

### bun run

Runs JavaScript & TypeScript on JavaScriptCore. Node.js APIs, node\_modules and your framework work as-is.

Replacesnodets-nodetsxnodemon

```
$ bun server.ts$ bun run dev$ bun --watch server.ts
```

[Runtime docs](https://bun.com/docs/cli/run)

### bun install

npm-compatible. Workspaces, catalogs, overrides, patches and a lockfile you can read.

## The APIs you need, baked in.

Most servers need an HTTP stack, a database client, Redis, S3, hashing and a way to shell out. Bun ships all of them, so that is a stack of packages you never install or patch.

Bun.serve() with routes, params and static responses.

[Docs](https://bun.com/docs/api/http)

server.ts

```
import { serve, sql } from "bun";

const server = serve({
  port: 3000,
  routes: {
    "/": new Response("Welcome to Bun!"),
    "/api/users/:id": async req => {
      const [user] = await sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`;
      return Response.json(user);
    },
  },
});

console.log(`Listening on ${server.url}`);
```

Turn your AI coding assistant into a full video production studio. Describe what you want in plain language — your agent handles research, scripting, asset generation, editing, and final composition.

**Important distinction:** OpenMontage can make image-based videos, but it can also make a real **video video** for free/open-source workflows: the agent builds a corpus from free stock footage and open archives, retrieves actual motion clips, edits them into a timeline, and renders a finished piece. That is not the usual "animate a handful of stills and call it video" trick.

**A service that creates a résumé based on your GitHub repos/activity.**

GitHub Résumé is **opt-in**. To make your resume visible, just **star** [this project](https://github.com/resume/resume.github.com). To view your résumé, go to `https://resume.github.io/?yourusername` or follow the instructions on the [home page](https://resume.github.io/).

Great for all the tech-savy bosses who want to have a **quick view** of person's git/github activity, *before the interview*.

**Mastodon is a non-profit that develops the Mastodon software.** Mastodon started in 2016 as an open-source project by Eugen Rochko, who, as an avid user since 2008, was dissatisfied with the state and direction of Twitter.

Believing that instant global communications were too crucial for modern society to belong to a single commercial company, he sought to build a user-friendly microblogging product that would not belong to any central authority, but remain practical for everyday use.

The first public launch occurred in October 2016. The initial support the project received through Patreon ensured that Eugen could begin working on the project full-time post-graduation. In April 2017 it received its first big break and garnered world-wide attention and press coverage.

The project was officially incorporated as a gGmbH (a German form of non-profit LLC) in 2021 but lost its non-profit status when Germany removed software projects from eligibility. In 2025, the team began the process of moving the project to a new foundation, and began implementing community governance.

The project was officially incorporated as a gGmbH (a German form of non-profit LLC) in 2021 but lost its non-profit status when Germany removed software projects from eligibility. # The React Foundation: A New Home for React Hosted by the Linux Foundation

February 24, 2026 by [Matt Carroll](https://x.com/mattcarrollcode)

![](https://react.dev/images/blog/react-foundation/react_foundation_logo.webp)![](https://react.dev/images/blog/react-foundation/react_foundation_logo_dark.webp)

The React Foundation has officially launched, hosted by the Linux Foundation.

---

[In October](https://react.dev/blog/2025/10/07/introducing-the-react-foundation), we announced our intent to form the React Foundation. Today, we’re excited to share that the React Foundation has officially launched.

React, React Native, and supporting projects like JSX are no longer owned by Meta — they are now owned by the React Foundation, an independent foundation hosted by the Linux Foundation. You can read more in the [Linux Foundation’s press release](https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-the-formation-of-the-react-foundation).

### Founding Members

The React Foundation has eight Platinum founding members: **Amazon**, **Callstack**, **Expo**, **Huawei**, **Meta**, **Microsoft**, **Software Mansion**, and **Vercel**. **Huawei** has joined since [our announcement in October](https://react.dev/blog/2025/10/07/introducing-the-react-foundation). The React Foundation will be governed by a board of directors composed of representatives from each member, with [Seth Webster](https://sethwebster.com/) serving as executive director.

![](https://react.dev/images/blog/react-foundation/react_foundation_member_logos_updated.webp)![](https://react.dev/images/blog/react-foundation/react_foundation_member_logos_dark_updated.webp)

### New Provisional Leadership Council

React’s technical governance will always be independent from the React Foundation board — React’s technical direction will continue to be set by the people who contribute to and maintain React. We have formed a provisional leadership council to determine this structure. We will share an update in the coming months.

## Status

**OpenCut is being rewritten from the ground up.** What's coming:

* An Editor API
* First-class third party plugins (made possible by a plugin-first architecture)
* Desktop, mobile, and browser from one codebase (Rust core)
* MCP server (for AI agents)
* Headless mode (automation, batch rendering)
* A scripting tab directly in the editor

You can still find the previous version at opencut-app/opencut-classic, which is the one to reach for today. opencut.app still runs the classic version. The rewrite will live at new.opencut.app until it's ready to take over.

## Development

Install proto if you haven't already:

**Linux, macOS, WSL:**

```
bash <(curl -fsSL https://moonrepo.dev/install/proto.sh)
```

**Windows (PowerShell):**

```
irm https://moonrepo.dev/install/proto.ps1 | iex
```

If shims fail to run, allow local scripts for your user:

```
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned
```

From the repo root:

```
proto use    # installs the tools pinned in .prototools
```

```
moon run web:dev       # localhost:5173
moon run api:dev       # localhost:8787
moon run desktop:dev   # see apps/desktop/README.md
```

We're not set up to take outside contributions yet while the architecture is being designed. If you want to follow along, ask questions, or just hang out, join the Discord or open an issue.

## Quick Start

> `dev` is the default branch and gets the newest changes first. Use `main` if you want the more curated branch.

```
git clone https://github.com/odysseus-dev/odysseus.git
cd odysseus
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d --build
```

Open `http://localhost:7011` when the containers are healthy. The first admin password is printed in `docker compose logs odysseus`.

The compose files pull the official multi-arch image `ghcr.io/odysseus-dev/odysseus` (published by CI on every push to `main` and `dev`) and only build locally if the pull fails — so this also works on hosts without a build toolchain, e.g. as a Portainer stack.

**Production deployments:** pin the immutable tag instead of `:latest`. `:latest` and bare `:X.Y.Z` tags move on every push to `main`, but `:X.Y.Z-<sha>` (e.g. `1.0.2-7c8070f`) always refers to one specific build:

```
ODYSSEUS_IMAGE=ghcr.io/odysseus-dev/odysseus:1.0.2-7c8070f docker compose up -d
```

Native installs, GPU notes, Windows/macOS instructions, HTTPS, and configuration live in the setup guide.

## About

PathSim is a Python framework for modeling continuous-time, discrete-time,
and hybrid dynamical systems as block diagrams. It targets engineers and
researchers who want a readable, scriptable alternative to traditional
simulation tools without giving up solver depth: more than thirty explicit,
implicit, and adaptive integrators, zero-crossing events and scheduled
triggers, hot-swappable blocks, and hierarchical subsystems. The only
runtime dependencies are numpy, scipy, and matplotlib.

Around the core sits a full ecosystem. PathView provides a visual
block-diagram editor in the browser, FastSim is a Rust engine with the
same API that also generates standalone C for embedded deployment, and
dedicated toolboxes cover chemical, battery, vehicle, flight, and RF
engineering. PathSim and its domain toolboxes are released under the MIT
license.

## Installation

## Ecosystem

pathview

Visual block diagram editor for building and simulating PathSim models in the browser.

fastsim

Fast Rust reimplementation of PathSim with an identical Python API and standalone C code generation for embedded deployment.

pathsim

Build and simulate continuous-time, discrete-time, and hybrid dynamical systems using block diagrams.

chem

Thermodynamic property correlations, activity coefficients, equations of state, and tritium processing.

batt

Battery cell blocks with PyBaMM integration for coupled electrothermal simulation.

vehicle

Tire models, suspension systems, and powertrain components for vehicle dynamics simulation.

flight

Six degrees of freedom equations of motion, aerodynamics, and propulsion for flight simulation.

rf

S-parameter networks, transmission lines, amplifiers, and mixers for RF and microwave simulation.

fmi

Wrap Co-Simulation and Model-Exchange FMUs (FMI 2.0 / 3.0) as PathSim blocks, driven by FMPy.

## Features

Hot-Swappable

Switch blocks and solvers during active simulation at runtime.

MIMO Capable

Multiple input, multiple output ports built into all blocks.

30+ Solvers

Implicit, explicit, and adaptive integrators for stiff and non-stiff systems.

Hierarchical

Nested subsystems for modular, reusable component design.

Event Handling

Zero-crossing detection and scheduled events for hybrid systems.

Extensible

Create custom blocks by subclassing the base Block class.

Browser Editor

Design and simulate visually with PathView using Pyodide.

Domain Toolboxes

Specialized blocks for chemical, vehicle, flight, and RF engineering.

## Introduction

This repo contains the algorithm infrastructure and some simple examples.

For the extended end-user products, please refer to the index repo Awesome-ChatTTS maintained by the community.  
You can find a diagram visualization of the codebase here.

ChatTTS is a text-to-speech model designed specifically for dialogue scenarios such as LLM assistant.

### Supported Languages

* English
* Chinese
* Coming Soon...

### Highlights

> You can refer to **this video on Bilibili** for the detailed description.

1. **Conversational TTS**: ChatTTS is optimized for dialogue-based tasks, enabling natural and expressive speech synthesis. It supports multiple speakers, facilitating interactive conversations.
2. **Fine-grained Control**: The model could predict and control fine-grained prosodic features, including laughter, pauses, and interjections.
3. **Better Prosody**: ChatTTS surpasses most of open-source TTS models in terms of prosody. We provide pretrained models to support further research and development.

PyCBC is a software package used to explore astrophysical sources of gravitational waves. It contains algorithms that can detect coalescing compact binaries and measure the astrophysical parameters of detected sources. Elixir v1.0 was released in September 2014 and a new minor version is released every 6 months, around June and December of every year. New releases are announced in the read-only [announcements mailing list](https://groups.google.com/group/elixir-lang-ann) and on the [GitHub releases page](https://github.com/elixir-lang/elixir/releases). Explain how a coding agent uses git worktrees, in three short paragraphs.

A worktree is a second checkout of the same repository that shares one .git directory. Each worktree sits on its own branch and has its own working files.

An agent creates one worktree per task. It can edit, run tests, and commit there without touching the branch you have open, so two tasks never fight over the same files.

When the task lands, the agent pushes the branch and opens a pull request. The worktree is deleted and the shared history stays clean.

# Go Micro

Go Micro is a Go framework for distributed systems development.

It provides RPC, service discovery, messaging, storage, and configuration.
Agents use services as tools to carry out work.
The gateway exposes services through HTTP and MCP for other applications and agents.
Each component uses a Go interface with a default implementation that can be replaced.

## Features

* **Services:** RPC with streaming, message encoding and service discovery.
* **Agents:** models, conversation history, tools, background tasks, and recovery.

## Getting started

Install the framework:

```
go get go-micro.dev/v6@latest
```

* Build and run a service — Go code and RPC; no model needed.
* Expose services to agents — connect your existing agent through MCP.
* Build a service with an agent — scaffold, run, and chat with your service.
* Chat with services — use Go Micro’s agent from the terminal.

Choose what you need. Chat does not require the gateway.

## Integrations

Browse integrations, propose one, or submit a listing PR. Community listings are free; sponsored placement and integration work help fund maintenance.

# OpenWork



OpenWork is the free, open-source alternative to Claude Cowork and Codex: a desktop app for macOS, Windows, and Linux where AI agents do real work on your own files. It is built on OpenCode, works with any model — 50+ providers, your own API keys, or local models via Ollama — and lets teams share skills and MCP servers.

**Download OpenWork** · GitHub releases · Docs

Read this in: 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · 日本語

Add one OpenWork MCP to Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, or another compatible agent and reuse the same skills, MCPs, and connected services across your tools, teammates, and machines. Create something once, share it with coworkers or friends, or keep it for yourself.

The desktop app is there when you want a dedicated workspace, but it is not required. You can use OpenWork from the agent you already have. For larger organizations, the admin interface lets you publish capabilities, manage access, and configure shared or per-user connections.



## Why OpenWork instead of Claude Cowork

* **Free and open source.** The desktop app is MIT-licensed; no OpenWork account is required to use it locally.
* **Any model.** Bring your own API key, sign in with ChatGPT, or run local models through Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible server. See Add a custom LLM.
* **Runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux** as a desktop app — not a CLI.
* **Your files stay local.** Cloud is optional.
* **Share skills and MCP servers with your team.** See Share skills with your team and Shared MCP connections.
* **Self-host** the team control plane on your own infrastructure. See Self-host.
* **Bring your Cowork setup.** Skills, Claude-compatible plugins, and MCP servers carry over. See Migrate from Claude Cowork.

## Install with your AI agent

Already use an AI agent? Copy this prompt and paste it into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ChatGPT, or any agent that can run commands on your computer.

```
Install OpenWork on my computer, set up my first workspace, and open it ready to use. Follow the steps in https://openworklabs.com/start.md?v=hero
```

1. Installs OpenWork
2. Creates your workspace
3. Opens it ready to run

## Use OpenWork from any agent

The OpenWork MCP brings your assigned skills, plugins, MCP connections, Google Workspace, and Microsoft 365 capabilities into any compatible agent.

It exposes four tools: `search_capabilities` finds what you can use, `execute_capability` runs it, and `list_skills` / `get_skill` list your skills and read one SKILL.md directly. After adding the MCP, your client opens a browser so you can sign in and choose your OpenWork organization.

### Codex

```
codex mcp add openwork --url https://api.openworklabs.com/mcp/agent
```

### Claude Code

```
claude mcp add --transport http openwork https://api.openworklabs.com/mcp/agent
```

### OpenCode

Add this to `opencode.json`:

```
{
  "mcp": {
    "openwork": {
      "type": "remote",
      "enabled": true,
      "url": "https://api.openworklabs.com/mcp/agent",
      "oauth": {}
    }
  }
}
```

### Any MCP client

Use this remote MCP server URL:

```
https://api.openworklabs.com/mcp/agent
```

## OpenWork Den

OpenWork Den is the control plane for managing OpenWork across a team or organization.

* Provision inference at scale and control which members and teams can use each model provider.
* Invite teammates, create teams, and manage access from one place.
* Set desktop policies, restrict local model access, and control which app versions your organization can use.
* Publish skills and plugins through marketplaces, then assign them to the organization, a team, or specific people.
* Import Agent Plugins or Anthropic-compatible plugins and make their supported skills and remote MCPs available through the OpenWork MCP.



## Licensing

This repository uses a directory-split license, similar to GitLab:

* **Everything outside `ee/` is MIT** — the desktop app and core platform are open source, free for any use.
* **Everything under `ee/` (OpenWork Den — the org control plane) is under the OpenWork EE License**, a source-available license. The code is public so you can audit exactly what you deploy. Production use requires an OpenWork subscription, except that it is **free for organizations with up to 5 users**, **free to evaluate for 30 days at any size**, and always free for development and testing. Each `ee/` release additionally converts to MIT two years after publication.

Versions released before this license was adopted remain under their original license (FSL-1.1-MIT). See pricing and the subscription terms.

## Documentation

Read the OpenWork docs.

## Getting started (contributors)

The fastest path from a fresh clone to a running dev build.

### Prerequisites

* **Node 24** — pinned in `.nvmrc` (`nvm use` picks it up).
* **pnpm 11** — pinned in `package.json` (`packageManager`); run `corepack enable` to use the pinned version automatically. Never use npm or yarn.

### First run

```
git clone https://github.com/different-ai/openwork.git
cd openwork
corepack enable
pnpm install
pnpm dev   # launches the Electron desktop app with hot reload
```

Coding agents and tests should not open that window on your screen: they use
the app in headless Chrome instead (see Headless web and `AGENTS.md`).

# Jujutsu—a version control system



   
  

**Homepage •**  **Installation •**  **Getting Started •**  **Development Roadmap •**  **Contributing**

## Introduction

Jujutsu is a powerful version control system for software projects. You use it to get a copy of your code, track changes
to the code, and finally publish those changes for others to see and use.
It is designed from the ground up to be easy to use—whether you're new or
experienced, working on brand new projects alone, or large scale software
projects with large histories and teams.

Jujutsu is unlike most other systems, because internally it abstracts the user
interface and version control algorithms from the *storage systems* used to
serve your content. This allows it to serve as a VCS with many possible physical
backends, that may have their own data or networking models—like Mercurial or Breezy, or hybrid systems like Google's cloud-based design, Piper/CitC.

Today, we use Git repositories as a storage layer to serve and track content,
making it **compatible with many of your favorite Git-based tools, right now!** However, note that only commits and files are stored in Git; bookmarks
(branches) and other higher-level metadata are stored in custom storage outside
of Git. All core developers use Jujutsu to develop Jujutsu, right here on
GitHub. But it should hopefully work with your favorite Git forges, too.

We combine many distinct design choices and concepts from other version control
systems into a single tool. Some of those sources of inspiration include:

* **Git**: We make an effort to be fast—with a snappy UX, efficient
    algorithms, correct data structures, and good-old-fashioned attention to
    detail. The default storage backend uses Git repositories for "physical
    storage", for wide interoperability and ease of onboarding.

* **Mercurial & Sapling**: There are many Mercurial-inspired features, such as
    the revset language to select commits. There is no explicit index or staging area. Branches are "anonymous" like Mercurial, so you don't need
    to make up a name for each small change. Primitives for rewriting history are
    powerful and simple. Formatting output is done with a robust template language
    that can be configured by the user.

* **Darcs**: Jujutsu keeps track of conflicts as first-class objects in its model; they are first-class in the same way commits
    are, while alternatives like Git simply think of conflicts as textual diffs.
    While not as rigorous as systems like Darcs (which is based on a formalized
    theory of patches, as opposed to snapshots), the effect is that many forms of
    conflict resolution can be performed and propagated automatically.

And it adds several innovative, useful features of its own:

* **Working-copy-as-a-commit**: Changes to files are recorded automatically as normal commits, and amended on every subsequent change. This "snapshot"
    design simplifies the user-facing data model (commits are the only visible
    object), simplifies internal algorithms, and completely subsumes features like
    Git's stashes or the index/staging-area.

* **Operation log & undo**: Jujutsu records every operation that is performed on the
    repository, from commits, to pulls, to pushes. This makes debugging problems like
    "what just happened?" or "how did I end up here?" easier, *especially* when
    you're helping your coworker answer those questions about their repository!
    And because everything is recorded, you can undo that mistake you just made
    with ease. Version control has finally entered the 1960s!

* **Automatic rebase and conflict resolution**: When you modify a commit, every
    descendent is automatically rebased on top of the freshly-modified one. This
    makes "patch-based" workflows a breeze. If you resolve a conflict in a commit,
    the *resolution* of that conflict is also propagated through descendants as
    well. In effect, this is a completely transparent version of `git rebase --update-refs` combined with `git rerere`, supported by design.

The following features are available for use, but experimental; they may have
bugs, backwards incompatible storage changes, and user-interface changes!

* **Safe, concurrent replication**: Have you ever wanted to store your version
    controlled repositories inside a Dropbox folder? Or continuously backup
    repositories to S3? No? Well, now you can!

    The fundamental problem with using filesystems like Dropbox and backup tools
    like `rsync` on your typical Git/Mercurial repositories is that they rely
    on *local filesystem operations* being atomic, serialized, and non-concurrent
    with respect to other reads and writes—which is *not* true when operating on
    distributed file systems, or when operations like concurrent file copies (for
    backup) happen while lock files are being held.

    Jujutsu is instead designed to be safe under concurrent scenarios;
    simply using rsync or Dropbox and then using that resulting repository
    should never result in a repository in a *corrupt state*. The worst that *should* happen is that it will expose conflicts between the local and remote
    state, leaving you to resolve them.

The command-line tool is called `jj` for now because it's easy to type and easy
to replace (rare in English). The project is called "Jujutsu" because it matches

# 8Q

[](https://github.com/Spooky-Manufacturing/8Q#contributors-)

[](https://zenodo.org/badge/latestdoi/275711975)

Computer with built-in General Purpose 8 Qubit Optical Quantum Processor

# Contributors

Thank you to all the contributors who make this possible

# Status: Moving Towards PCB!

We're beginning to layout the components and finalize the design of our quantum computer! As we continue to design the PCB, we are also working with optical engineers to make our logic gates more compact which will enable us to shrink the design even further than we already have!

### Development Board

To speed up R&D, we've decided to replace the ARM CPU with a QSeven2.0 spec'd "computer on module". There are a variety of benefits to doing this, one major benefit being that we can switch between a variety of x86 and ARM processors.

The current design effort utilizes the Congatech A50 CoM.

[](https://github.com/Spooky-Manufacturing/8Q/blob/master/docs/source/imgs/cpu.png)

### Quantum Processing Unit

[](https://github.com/Spooky-Manufacturing/8Q/blob/master/docs/source/imgs/qpu.png)

### QController

The QController acts as a bridge between the main (digital) computer and the quantum processor. It is responsible for storing/executing instructions, and for transferring data to/from the host and QPU.

## Features

[](https://github.com/Spooky-Manufacturing/8Q/blob/master/docs/source/imgs/8q.png)

* Quad-Core Cortex-A53
* Mali-T720 MP2 GPU
* 1x DDR4 Ram Slot (Max 64GB)
* 32/64 Bit Compatible
* Linux Capable

##### 🔴 Note: SaProt (35M and 650M) requires structural (SA token) input for optimal performance. Its AA-only sequence mode works but should be finetuned - its frozen embeddings work only for SA input, not AA sequences! In contrast, SaProt-1.3B (SaProt\_1.3B\_AF2 & SaProt\_1.3B\_AFDB\_OMG\_NCBI) performs well with both SA tokens and AA-only sequences. ## AKFamily
专注于财经数据与量化投研的开源社区。从获取数据到回测与实盘，提供一套开源免费的 Python 工具链。
AKShare（获取财经数据） → AKTools（HTTP API 与 MCP 服务） → AKQuant（量化回测与实盘）
