== brainlife https://brainlife.io/docs/
Anyone can develop, use, combine, and reuse Apps to build complex pipelines for customized brain data analyses on the platform. You can publish apps to be used privately or shared publicly with the brainlife.io community. Combining multiple Apps allows for high-throughput data processing and aggregation across thousands of datasets.
The best way to manage your data is with brainlife.io’s Projects feature. Here you can organize your datasets, perform data processing, and share results with your team by granting varying levels of access to members of your group. Projects can be public or private.
brainlife Datatypes are maintained by individual developers and are updated at [brainlife.io](https://brainlife.io/datatypes).
Our compute resources are unique because, instead of running an entire workflow on a single resource, App developers can identify the best resource for each individual App by scoring brainlife.io’s compute resources on how well they work with each App. brainlife.io automatically keeps track of success rate and time to compute so that users can easily see how efficiently each resource processes data for each App.
Users can perform data visualizations on brainlife.io in the cloud instead of on their own computer, which means better security and data management. Data visualization gives users feedback on the quality of the results generated by Apps and pipelines. The visualizations allow users to run popular software for data visualization like FreeView, FSLview, or MRview. Users can additionally run GPU-rendered visualizations on the cloud through Docker and VNC. Similar to Apps, developers can contribute visualizations to the platform.

# K-Dense BYOK

          

> ### 🎥 Webinar recording: **Getting Started with K-Dense BYOK**
> 
> An online walkthrough of installing Kady and running your first research task, with live Q&A.
> 
> 👉 **Watch the recording on YouTube**

**Your own AI research assistant, running on your computer, powered by the accounts and API keys you choose.**

   

K-Dense BYOK (Bring Your Own Keys) is a free, open-source app that gives you **Kady** — an AI research assistant for scientists in any field. Describe a task in plain language — *analyze this dataset*, *review my manuscript*, *search the literature*, *build this figure* — and Kady works through it in a complete research workspace. It can inspect your files, write and run analysis code, search and read sources, create figures and reports, and keep a living record of what it did.

Four things to know up front:

* **No coding experience required.** You describe what you want; Kady writes and runs the code and shows you its progress as it works.
* **Every step is on the record.** Kady keeps a lab notebook of its reasoning and a separate, automatically recorded log of what actually ran and which files each step produced, so results can be checked, traced, and reproduced.
* **Your workspace stays on your computer.** Projects, conversations, notebooks, and results live in ordinary folders on your machine; K-Dense does not host or store them. When you use a hosted AI model, the material needed for that request is sent directly to the provider you selected under that provider's privacy terms. Use a local Ollama model when data must not leave your machine.
* **The app itself is free; provider charges and limits remain yours.** Use prepaid OpenRouter, connect a supported AI subscription, or run free local models. Kady tracks paid OpenRouter usage and Anthropic OAuth's documented metered extra usage against project spending caps. ChatGPT, Copilot, xAI, Kimi Code, and Meta Muse subscription usage is tracked separately because those providers manage quotas and overages; a subscription login does not imply unlimited or free usage.

> **Beta:** K-Dense BYOK is currently in beta. Many features and improvements are on the way. Star us on GitHub to stay in the loop, and follow K-Dense on X, LinkedIn, YouTube, and Reddit for release notes and tutorials.

> 🎬 **Prefer to watch first?** The Future of Research is Open: Introducing K-Dense BYOK walks through what the app does and how to get set up. More walkthroughs in Tutorial videos.

> 📄 **Read the paper:** K-Dense BYOK: An Open-Source AI Research Assistant That Runs Locally and Keeps a Hash-Chained Lab Notebook (arXiv:2610.00074). If you use K-Dense BYOK in your research, please cite it.

## CompBioBench

As of September 11, 2026, K-Dense BYOK holds **\#2** on the public CompBioBench v1 leaderboard.

CompBioBench is a Genentech benchmark of 100 computational-biology tasks. Each task has one exact-match answer. The gold answers stay on the leaderboard, so an independent grader scores every run.

We ran the same K-Dense BYOK harness four times through OpenRouter. Each run used one model and one isolated project per question.


Ranks will move as new submissions arrive. For agreement, failures, and cost on the first three runs, see K-Dense BYOK on CompBioBench.

## Internal benchmark



This figure compares K-Dense BYOK, Claude Science, and Biomni Lab across scientific quality and research execution in a 20-prompt benchmark. # T3 Code

The open-source control plane for coding agents.

**Download** · iOS · Android · Web · Docs · Discord



T3 Code runs the coding agents on your machine and gives them one fast interface. Start a thread at your desk, then approve the next step from your phone.

It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build, Antigravity, Kiro, Pi, Muse Code, fx, and any ACP agent. If an agent is set up on your computer, T3 Code can control it.

## What you get

* **Your subscriptions.** T3 Code does not resell tokens. It drives the agents you are already signed in to.
* **Every agent in one place.** Change models in the middle of a thread. Let Claude hand a task to Codex.
* **Desktop, web, and phone.** One server, and every client shows the same threads. There are apps for iOS and Android.
* **Remote ready.** Run agents on any machine. Connect over your local network, Tailscale, or T3 Connect.
* **Git built in.** Each thread can work in its own worktree. Review the diff, then commit, push, and open a pull request with one button.
* **Fast.** Performance is a feature here. We measure it, and we treat a dropped frame as a bug.
* **Open.** Source code is MIT licensed. If you don't like something, fork it under your own branding (see Trademarks and forks).

## Install

### Desktop app

Download T3 Code for macOS, Windows, or Linux. You can also use a package manager:


### Command line

This installs the `t3` command. Run `t3` to start the server and open the web app.

```
curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```
irm https://t3.codes/install.ps1 | iex
```

To try it once without an install, run `npx t3@latest`.

### Phone

Get the app from the App Store or Google Play. Then follow remote access to connect it to your computer.

### Sign in to an agent

T3 Code needs one agent that is installed and signed in. For example, install Claude Code and run `claude auth login`, or install Codex CLI and run `codex login`.

Provider setup has the steps for each agent. Install T3 Code covers nightly builds, AppImage, WSL, and NixOS.

## "Wait, what are you selling me?"

Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork the source code and build the tool that you want, under your own name and branding.

## Documentation

* Install and first run
* Remote access from a phone or another machine
* Permission modes
* Source control
* Connect outside agents over MCP
* FAQ

All docs has the full list.

## Contributing

We have limited review capacity. Small, focused fixes are the most likely to be merged. Features need an approved discussion first.

* Read CONTRIBUTING.md before you report a bug or open a pull request.
* Put feature requests in Ideas.
* Build from source with the development runbook. The architecture overview explains how it works.
* Get help in Discord.

import hashlib
out=Path('/workspace/owner_class_audit.csv')
audit.to_csv(out,index=False,encoding='utf-8',lineterminator='\n')
hardest=['Spooky-Manufacturing','OpenMontageInc','labmlai','micro','K-Dense-AI','Textualize','php','spacetelescope','mixOmics-org']
notes=[]
notes += ['# Owner classification audit', '', f'Primary-source checks: {datetime.date.today().isoformat()}.', '',
'I classified all 120 accounts in the original input order, using the seven columns requested in the task. I checked at least one organization website or repository for every account and attached a checked primary URL to every row. I used account identity, governance, and the relationship between open projects and paid products or services. I did not query or use financial outcomes to choose classes.', '',
'## Counts', '', '| Class | Accounts |', '|---|---:|']
for c,n in counts.items(): notes.append(f'| `{c}` | {int(n)} |')
notes += ['| **Total** | **120** |', '',f'**Judgment calls: {int(audit.judgment.sum())}. Unknown accounts: 0.** These are unweighted sample counts, not estimates of the distribution across all popular GitHub organizations. The sample contains 60 accounts from the top 300 and 60 from the remainder.', '',
'## Hardest classifications', '']
for o in hardest:
 r=rows[o]
 notes.append(f"- **`{o}` → `{r['cls']}`:** {judgment_notes[o]} [Checked source]({r['source_url']}).")
notes += ['', '## Every account marked `judgment=1`', '',
'The table includes all judgment calls, in input order. A flag marks a discretionary boundary or incomplete ownership evidence; it does not imply that the owner is wholly unidentified.', '',
'| Owner | Class | Reason | Checked sources |','|---|---|---|---|']
for o in x.owner:
 if o in judgment_notes:
  links='; '.join(f"[Source {i+1}]({ev['url']})" for i,ev in enumerate(evidence[o]))
  notes.append(f"| `{o}` | `{rows[o]['cls']}` | {judgment_notes[o]} | {links} |")
notes += ['', '## Decisions and limitations', '',
'- I classify the organization account, not a repository’s topic, its contributors’ employers, or its sponsors. I do not treat institutional affiliations alone as ownership.',
'- I distinguish a foundation’s legal stewardship from fiscal hosting or other support. I apply the supplied community examples even when a project has an organizational sponsor.',
'- I apply the explicit project-home/maintainer-company tie-breaker where a commercial provider offers the project’s hosted, enterprise, licensed, or support variant. I flag borderline applications.',
'- I use current ownership statements. React’s official announcement explicitly places React and React Native under the React Foundation, hosted by the Linux Foundation; the lysine-dev account identifies itself as a Commonhaus member. I do not preserve their historical corporate associations as their current class.',
'- I leave `parent` blank when no different ultimate parent is established. A corporate entity can remain core or complement even where its ultimate parent is a nonprofit foundation.',
'- I use `unknown` only when the owner cannot be identified at all. For named but legally informal project groups, I choose the more likely class and flag uncertainty when appropriate. Zero unknowns should not be read as proof that every organization’s legal title was verified.',
'- Public pages establish product and governance relationships more reliably than legal title or organization-account administration. Some named legal entities and paid-product links remain unverified; the judgment notes identify these gaps. A failed website fetch is a verification limitation, not evidence about an owner’s business status.',
'- This is one independent rules-based audit, not a legal due-diligence review or an inter-rater reliability study. No comparison labels were provided, so I do not report agreement or accuracy.',
'- I use product descriptions and commercial offerings to distinguish core from complement without measuring financial outcomes. For product-boundary cases, the chosen class is explicitly a judgment, not a measured commercial mix.', '',
'## Validation', '',
'- Exactly 120 output rows, with one row for every input owner and no duplicates.',
'- Owner order exactly matches `audit_sample.csv`.',
'- Exact columns: `owner,cls,entity,parent,basis,judgment,source_url`.',
'- Every `basis` has at most 15 whitespace-delimited words; every judgment flag is 0 or 1.',
'- Every output source URL was successfully fetched in this audit.', '']
notes_path=Path('/workspace/owner_class_audit_notes.md')
notes_path.write_text('\n'.join(notes),encoding='utf-8')
# Round-trip validation of the actual delivered CSV.
reloaded=pd.read_csv(out,keep_default_na=False)
assert list(reloaded.columns)==['owner','cls','entity','parent','basis','judgment','source_url']
assert len(reloaded)==120 and reloaded.owner.tolist()==x.owner.tolist()
assert reloaded.owner.is_unique
assert reloaded.cls.isin(classes).all()
assert reloaded.entity.str.len().gt(0).all()
assert reloaded.basis.str.split().str.len().le(15).all()
assert reloaded.judgment.isin([0,1]).all()
assert reloaded.source_url.str.startswith('https://').all()
assert reloaded.equals(audit)
assert int(counts.sum())==120
support=Path('/workspace/audit_support');support.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(support/'source_index.json').write_text(json.dumps(source_index,ensure_ascii=False,indent=2),encoding='utf-8')
(support/'judgment_notes.json').write_text(json.dumps(judgment_notes,ensure_ascii=False,indent=2),encoding='utf-8')
def sha(p): return hashlib.sha256(Path(p).read_bytes()).hexdigest()
validation={'rows':120,'classes':counts.to_dict(),'judgment_calls':int(audit.judgment.sum()),'columns':audit.columns.tolist(),'all_input_owners_in_original_order':True,'basis_max_words':int(audit.basis.str.split().str.len().max()),'accounts_with_checked_sources':len(evidence),'checked_primary_pages':len(source_index),'sha256':{str(p):sha(p) for p in [Path('/workspace/audit_sample.csv'),Path('/workspace/classify_rules.md'),out]}}
(support/'validation.json').write_text(json.dumps(validation,indent=2),encoding='utf-8')
manifest={'files':[{'path':str(out),'description':'All 120 independent owner classifications in input order, with the requested seven columns.','kind':'final'},{'path':str(notes_path),'description':'Class counts, hardest classifications, explanations of all 36 judgment calls, source links and limitations.','kind':'final'},{'path':str(support/'source_index.json'),'description':'Checked primary-source index and saved citation keys.','kind':'intermediate'},{'path':str(support/'judgment_notes.json'),'description':'Machine-readable explanations of discretionary classifications.','kind':'intermediate'},{'path':str(support/'validation.json'),'description':'Executed output validations and input/output hashes.','kind':'intermediate'}]}
for p in citation_paths:
 manifest['files'].append({'path':p,'description':'Saved full BibTeX entries for checked primary sources.','kind':'intermediate'})
Path('/workspace/.deliverables.json').write_text(json.dumps(manifest,indent=2))
print(json.dumps(validation,indent=2))
print('\nCSV first lines:\n'+'\n'.join(out.read_text().splitlines()[:6]))
print('\nFinal files:',out.name,notes_path.name)

info.problem: You are auditing a classification step in a pre-registered study of who owns popular open-source software. audit_sample.csv lists 120 GitHub organization accounts (60 drawn at random from the 300 with the most stars, 60 from the rest), with each account's name, website, e-mail domain, location, creation year, description and top repositories. classify_rules.md gives the classes (core, complement, nonprofit, academic, government, community, unknown) and the tie-breakers. Classify every account independently by those rules, checking the organization's website or repository where you are unsure. Do not use any financial outcome (funding, valuation, revenue, acquisition price, shutdown) to decide a class. Output a CSV named owner_class_audit.csv with columns owner, cls, entity, parent, basis (at most 15 words), judgment (1 if a judgment call), source_url, one row per input account in input order, and report the counts by class and the accounts you found hardest to classify, with reasons.
